sentences.text: Lagerpeton is a reptile whose name combines the Greek words for 'hare' and 'reptile'.
This animal was about 70 cm long and weighed less than 4 kg, estimates derived from its hind limb measurements and reduced bone cross-sections.
It possessed a narrow foot with only two functional toes and an unusually elongated fourth toe.
Scientists have identified twenty-one unique anatomical characters specific to this species.
Lagerpeton lacks key dinosaurian features like the anterior trochanter, placing it at the base of Dinosauromorpha or potentially outside the group entirely.
The animal possesses anteriorly inclined neural spines on its dorsal vertebrae, a feature common in leaping mammals but unique among archosaurs.
Its pelvic girdle is remarkably small relative to its hindlimb length.
Artistic reconstructions depict the animal in a dynamic running posture supported by its notably long and thin single hind leg.
Lagerpeton was first described by Alfred S. Romer in 1971 from fossils found in the Chañares Formation of Argentina, based on a complete right hind limb.
All known Lagerpeton fossils have been found exclusively in the Chañares Formation of La Rioja Province, Argentina.
A smaller specimen, MCZ 4121, was described by Romer in 1972 and was preserved in a nodule alongside fossils of Lewisuchus and Lagosuchus.
Andrea Arcucci described two additional specimens, PVL 4619 and PVL 4625, in 1986.
Researchers suggest that modern small bipedal mammals that leap are the closest living analogues to Lagerpeton.
The hypothesis that Lagerpeton was a leaping animal is currently debated among scientists, as some argue the small pelvic girdle and reduced toes could instead indicate a running lifestyle.
The parent group of Lagerpeton is Lagerpetidae.
Lagerpeton is related to Dromomeron, which lived during the Late Triassic in the southwestern United States.
The oldest Lagerpeton fossils date to the Upper Middle Triassic (Ladinian) period and were found in Gondwana, part of southern Pangaea, living between 241.464 and 237 million years ago.
Radiometric dating places the Chañares Formation and its fossils between 236 and 234 million years old.

Footprints from Poland dating to the Early to Late Olenekian show a quadrupedal dinosauromorph similar to Lagerpeton; if these belong to a close relative, the group's origins could be pushed back to the Early Triassic, challenging the theory that bipedalism was the ancestral state for dinosaurs.

The hypothesis that Lagerpeton was a leaping animal is currently debated among scientists, as some argue the small pelvic girdle and reduced toes could instead indicate a running lifestyle rather than leaping.
